proposed_edges.relationship: Fitzpatrick names Carr as one of the two scholars in England who ‘knew something about’ her planned doctoral research and encouraged it, and recalls admiring him and his way of working (interview, 2012); Menashe (1996) counts Carr among the ‘spiritual godfathers’ of revisionism, a movement in which he singles out her work.
proposed_edges.map_label: Carr and the young Fitzpatrick; revisionism's godfather
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Her own words, read 2026-10-31. Baltic Worlds interview (BW 1, 2012, print pp. 4–10; conducted 5 January 2012; interviewer not named on the page), answer on her doctoral years: ‘The two people who knew something about what I wanted to do were E. H. Carr in Cambridge and Leonard Schapiro at the London School of Economics’; ‘I admired Carr. I found him to be a fascinating figure’; ‘I was quite fascinated by his way of working which was completely different from mine’; she adds that ‘Carr was remote’ and that, writing on politics and economics in the 1920s, ‘he had the sources’. The editorial sidebar (not her words) calls Carr ‘one of Sheila Fitzpatrick's mentors during her stay in England’. A named reader, read: Louis Menashe, ‘Revising the Revisionists’, ILWCH 50 (1996), note 1 (displayed reference note on the Cambridge page): ‘Spiritual godfathers of revisionism were Isaac Deutscher and E. H. Carr’, Carr for his ‘insistence on value-free explorations of Soviet society’; the same note says the study of popular support was ‘a project undertaken with the greatest skill by Sheila Fitzpatrick’ (citing Education and Social Mobility, 1978, and The Russian Revolution, 1982). Limits: personal admiration and early support, and one reader's genealogy of revisionism; she stresses that her method differed from his. No supervision, co-authorship or adoption of Carr's political judgements is claimed. Her memoir A Spy in the Archives (2013; MUP blurb read, no Carr mention) and the LRB essay of the same title (2010, read, no Carr mention) do not add evidence; Menashe's article body unread (no abstract; first page an image). Reviewer 2026-10-31: same answer adds ‘I spoke to those two people and both of them were very encouraging to me’ and ‘we got quite friendly, I think’.

proposed_edges.relationship: Everyday Stalinism (1999) asks how Soviet city dwellers managed ordinary lives in the extraordinary conditions of the 1930s, and the joint chapter with Alf Lüdtke (2008) takes the everyday in Nazi Germany and Stalinist Russia as the ground on which to test Arendt's atomization thesis, asking whether social relationships broke down and were perhaps reconfigured.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Read 2026-10-31. A reader of the book: J. Arch Getty, ‘Palaces on Monday’, LRB 22:5 (2 March 2000), review of Everyday Stalinism, full text: ¶1 the shift from the ‘totalitarian model’ to a ‘new Soviet social history’ that ‘insisted that society mattered, even in dictatorships’; ¶4 ‘Strictly empirical analysis is her preferred method’; ¶6 the book's question, ‘how did ordinary people manage?’; ¶9 shopping as, ‘in Fitzpatrick's phrase, a “survival skill”’. Joint chapter (Cambridge page summary, read): Fitzpatrick and Lüdtke, ‘Energizing the Everyday: On the Breaking and Making of Social Bonds in Nazism and Stalinism’, in Geyer and Fitzpatrick, eds., Beyond Totalitarianism (2008), pp. 266–301, takes ‘the everyday in Nazi Germany and Stalinist Russia’ as the place where relationships broke and were possibly reconfigured; Lüdtke is the Alltagsgeschichte figure named on the micro node. Her own caveat (Baltic Worlds 2012, read): Everyday Stalinism is ‘a very atheoretical book. There is all this theory on the everyday, and I pay little attention to it.’ So the edge records a contribution to the history of everyday life, not adherence to Alltagsgeschichte or microstoria method. The book itself is unread; the existing social and Arendt edges (edge_2916, edge_2918) already use the joint chapter for different claims. Reviewer 2026-10-31: the Cambridge summary's wording is that the authors took Arendt's atomization hypothesis as the ‘starting point for our comparative inquiry into the everyday in Nazi Germany and Stalinist Russia that in each case some kind of breakdown (but perhaps also a reconfiguration?) of social relationships took place’; ‘remade’ is not claimed.

Baltic Worlds: 'a very atheoretical book. There is all this theory on the everyday, and I pay little attention to it.' Cambridge chapter summary re-fetched: 'some kind of breakdown (but perhaps also a reconfiguration?) of social relationships', framed as a test of Arendt's atomization hypothesis. The relationship's 'a site where social bonds broke and were remade' overstates the tentative 'perhaps also a reconfiguration?'. Edit accordingly; add closing period. The micro node is 'Microhistory / everyday life' and the edge is explicitly a contribution to everyday-life history, not microstoria method, which the evidence note says.

edges_considered_not_proposed.reason: Baltic Worlds 2012: ‘When I read The Presentation of Self in Everyday Life, I didn't think about it as theory’; she took it as confirming how she already saw the world. Affinity she reports, not a debt; held.
Baltic Worlds 2012: ‘Bourdieu is one, but I read him too late to have him as an inspiration.’ Her own words rule out influence; not proposed.

Getty (LRB 2000, ¶4) says she is ‘doubtful of the explanatory force of Foucault's multiple discourses of power’, and the Baltic Worlds sidebar quotes her distinguishing Tear Off the Masks! from the Foucauldian ‘Soviet subjectivity’ school. A reader's one-line characterisation and a disagreement with Foucault's later Soviet readers, not with Foucault; her own text unread. Held.
Mazower reviewed Mischka's War in the LRB (7 February 2019; listing seen, review not read). A book review alone is not a relationship of note; not investigated further.
